newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION - Jim Middleton's Canberra Close-up - Shoot the messenger.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Jim Middleton's Canberra Close-up - Shoot the messenger.

text.p: Jim Middleton (ABC TV political correspondent)
"I'm in charge ..." the words of Alexander Haig -- then U.S. Secretary of State at the time of the assassination attempt.
In fact, he wasn't in charge and soon after he wasn't Secretary of State either. But his phrase lives on and could now be applied to the Howard government and its recent behaviour.

The Mortimer Report into business assistance was finally made public on Wednesday. David Mortimer -- the TNT chief responsible for the review -- made himself available to discuss the reasons behind its findings. Not so, Industry Minister John Moore, who is charged with managing the government's response.

Apart from hinting that he thought Mortimer was behind well informed leaks in the morning papers he confined himself to declaring the report could be "a cornerstone" for future government economic policy.

Treasurer Peter Costello felt no such constraint. Two and a half hours before the report's release he weighed into the review's key recommendation -- that the government formally commit itself to doubling the country's average growth rate from 1.7 percent to 3.4 percent.
The Howard government has shied away from fixed economic targets like Dracula from a stake and Costello was not about to change his habits.

"Look, I don't think there's any point in sitting around and having particular numbers for growth targets," he declared. "I don't think any government's done that in Australia for a long time and I don't believe any would."
Quite a whack.
Why Moore had not been prepared to speak up for the report -- even in general terms -- mystified more than a few seasoned industry observers.
Not to do so means that Costello was left to make the running and now Moore will have to work overtime to catch up.
The incident is not likely to please those business figures who've been pushing for a more activist industry policy and will see Costello's outburst as a pre-emptive bid to kill off any such moves.
When Moore did finally pipe up -- on the ABC's 7.30 Report last night -- he was on the defensive.
The news he made was not in his portfolio area but on tax, where he declared that the government would come up with a "co-ordinated approach" to tax reform.
That goes further than any commitments so far from Howard or Costello and neither is likely to thank him for his contribution because it unnecessarily advances expectations.
But it's far from an isolated episode.

During the last session of parliament the prime minister suggested tax reform could boost jobs. That night his treasurer denied it. Last week, Howard promoted the idea of free trade zones to kick start investment. This week Costello poured cold water on the idea. Remind you of another prime minister and his treasurer, perhaps?

Then there's the debacle of those leaked briefing papers -- whose existence was revealed to the world by Reuters. It was the Treasury which made the blunder, but the man initially left to pick up the pieces was Foreign Minister Alexander Downer.
It was a full three days after the leak before Costello made public comment on the fiasco.

And then there was little sign of any contrition. Instead the treasurer tried to shoot the messenger, claiming publication was not in the national interest. Shades of the efforts of Paul Keating's staff to intimidate reporters when he branded Malaysia's Mahathir Mohamed a "recalcitrant."

No wonder a foreign affairs E-mail attacking the authors of the document and distancing the department mysteriously happened to be stapled to an official briefing note on an entirely different subject handed out to journalists on Wednesday.
Sceptics are wondering just how such an "accident" could have happened. It all looked more like foreign affairs self defence and inter-departmental retribution.

And what of the contents of the leaked paper? What does it say about the calibre of the Office of National Assessments that such crude estimates are made of the leaders of Australia's nearest neighbours? If they write such things about them, what are they thinking about other countries and competitors on whom Australia depends for its export income? Is it time for heads to roll?

It's also notable that a week after the debacle not one Australian minister has publicly expressed any regret. Not Costello, not Downer, not Howard. No wonder that by yesterday tempers were starting to fray across the Tasman. Winston Peters, branded "opportunist" who spent too much time in night clubs called the authors dingoes, a fellow New Zealand Minister dubbed them "mongrels."
As these episodes demonstrate, this government's modus operandi is reactive not pro-active. It appears to have tactics rather than strategy. Who is in charge?
-- Canberra Reuters Bureau 61-6 273-2730
